blocks.text: Every previous lesson in this module, tools, resources, and prompts, ultimately exists to put useful information in front of a model. This lesson steps back and looks at context itself, the total picture of everything a model actually sees when it is asked to respond, and how tools, resources, and prompts each contribute to shaping it.
1. What Context Means in an MCP Session

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Tools and resources both feed into context

blocks.text: Context is everything a model has available to it when generating a response, the conversation so far, any system instructions, the results of tool calls it made, and the content of any resources that were read in. None of this is permanent or automatic, it has to be deliberately assembled and kept relevant.

blocks.title: A useful framing
blocks.content: If it is not in context for this specific request, the model simply does not know it, no matter how obviously true or recently discussed it might seem to a human following along.

blocks.text: This is exactly why an assistant can sometimes seem to forget something mentioned earlier in a very long conversation, it is not truly forgetting, that piece of context was simply trimmed to make room for newer information.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you are ever unsure why a model gave a strange answer, the first question worth asking is, what did its context actually contain at that moment.

blocks.text: 2. Context Has a Limited Size

A model’s context window, covered in full depth in its own dedicated lesson in the Context Management module, is finite, everything contributing to context, conversation history, tool results, resource content, has to fit within that limit, making context a genuinely scarce resource to budget carefully rather than fill without thought.
Different models have very different context window sizes, some measured in the low thousands of tokens, others in the hundreds of thousands, but every single one of them has some limit.

code.content:
# a rough estimate of how much of the window is already used
used_tokens = estimate_tokens(system_prompt) + estimate_tokens(conversation_history)
remaining_tokens = context_window_size - used_tokens

blocks.text: Knowing roughly how large a target model’s context window is, even approximately, is a genuinely useful piece of information to keep in mind while designing any MCP-based application.
3. Tools Contribute Context Through Their Results

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A tool result gets added to context

blocks.text: Every time a tool is called, its result becomes part of the ongoing context, a weather lookup’s result stays available to the model for the rest of that conversation, unless it is deliberately dropped or summarized away later.

code.content:
# a second tool call, its result also joining context
result2 = client.call_tool("get_weather", {"city": "Delhi"})
conversation_context.append({"role": "tool", "content": result2})

blocks.text: If a tool is called many times across a long session, each result accumulating in context, a host needs to think about whether older, now-irrelevant results should eventually be dropped.
A host might also choose to summarize an especially large or verbose tool result before it is added to context, applying the same discipline used for oversized resources.
4. Resources Contribute Context Through Their Content

Reading a resource pulls its content directly into context, a large resource can consume a meaningful chunk of the available space all at once, which is exactly why resource size and relevance matter so much, covered in the Resources Can Be Large lesson earlier in this module.

This is exactly why a client might choose to summarize a large resource before inserting it into context, rather than pasting in the entire raw content and consuming far more space than the task actually needs.

code.content:
# summarizing before inserting into context
full_doc = client.read_resource("file:///large_report.txt")
summary = summarize(full_doc["text"], max_length=500)
conversation_context.append({"role": "resource", "content": summary})

blocks.text: A resource read early in a session that no longer has any bearing on the current question is a reasonable candidate to trim, exactly the same judgment call described for tool results.
5. Prompts Shape Context by Framing the Request

A filled-in prompt becomes part of the message context too, often the very instruction the model responds to, prompts do not just add raw content, they frame how the model should interpret everything else already present in context.

A well-designed prompt template essentially pre-writes the framing so a user does not have to construct it themselves, letting the same clear instruction appear consistently no matter who triggers it.

blocks.title: A useful way to see it
blocks.content: A resource supplies the what, a prompt often supplies the how, together they give the model both the raw material and the instruction for what to do with it.

code.content:
# the filled prompt becomes the framing message in context
filled = client.get_prompt("summarize_document", {"document_text": doc_text})
context.append(filled["messages"][0])

blocks.text: 6. Conversation History Is Also Context

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Conversation history is part of context

blocks.text: Beyond tools, resources, and prompts, the ordinary back-and-forth of a conversation itself accumulates as context, every prior user message and every prior model response takes up space, which is why a very long conversation can eventually crowd out room for new tool results or resource content.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Contributor","Grows over time"],"rows":[["Conversation history","Yes, every turn adds more"],["A single tool result","No, fixed once received"],["A single resource read","No, fixed once received"]]}

blocks.text: This is one reason very long-running conversations, covered in the Long-Running Sessions lesson later in this curriculum, need deliberate strategies for summarizing or trimming history rather than letting it grow forever.

code.content:
# a simple trimming strategy, keep only the last N turns
conversation_context = conversation_context[-20:]

blocks.text: A simple sliding window, keeping only the most recent turns, is a common starting strategy, though it risks losing something important said much earlier, more thoughtful approaches are covered in Context Compression.
7. Not All Context Is Equally Relevant

A tool result from early in a long conversation may no longer matter by the time a new, unrelated question is asked, part of managing context well is recognizing when older information has become irrelevant and can be safely left out of what gets sent to the model going forward.
Deciding what to drop is a judgment call, dropping too aggressively risks losing something the model actually still needed, dropping too little risks running out of space at an inconvenient moment.

blocks.title: A helpful heuristic
blocks.content: If the current question has nothing to do with an earlier tool result, that result is a reasonable first candidate to drop when space is needed.

blocks.text: This same judgment call reappears constantly throughout building real MCP based applications, relevance is rarely a fixed, permanent property, it shifts as the conversation itself moves on to new topics.
8. Who Decides What Goes Into Context

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A host decides what goes into context

blocks.text: The host application, not the MCP server and not the model itself, is ultimately responsible for assembling context, deciding what conversation history, tool results, and resource content to include in any given request to the model.

This is one of the host application’s most important, and least visible, responsibilities, a well-built host manages this quietly and effectively, a poorly built one lets context bloat unchecked or drops something important by accident.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Layer","Responsibility"],"rows":[["Model","Reasons over whatever context it is given"],["Host","Decides exactly what that context contains"]]}

blocks.text: This is also why two different host applications connected to the exact same MCP servers can still produce noticeably different quality results, the difference often comes down to how thoughtfully each one manages context.
9. Stale Context Can Mislead a Model

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Stale context can mislead a model

blocks.text: If a resource was read once and its content has since changed, but the model is still working from the old, cached version in context, it can confidently reason from information that is no longer accurate, this is exactly the problem the Context Synchronization lesson in the Context Management module addresses.

code.content:
# a naive cache that never refreshes
cached_doc = client.read_resource("file:///status.txt")   # read once, early in the session
# ... file is edited elsewhere ...
# model still reasons from the old cached_doc unless it is re-read

blocks.text: A more careful host might re-check a resource’s freshness before relying on a previously cached read, especially for anything time-sensitive like a status or a price.

blocks.title: A safeguard worth building
blocks.content: Some systems attach a timestamp to cached resource content, and re-read automatically if that timestamp is older than some acceptable threshold.

blocks.text: The right refresh frequency depends entirely on how quickly the underlying data actually changes, a slowly changing configuration file needs far less frequent re-reading than a live status feed.
10. A Simple Mental Model for Context

It can help to picture context as a whiteboard with a fixed amount of space, every tool result, every piece of resource content, every message adds something to that whiteboard, and once it is full, something old has to be erased to make room for something new.

blocks.title: Extending the whiteboard analogy
blocks.content: A good host is like a thoughtful person managing that whiteboard, erasing what is clearly no longer needed, and never letting truly important information get pushed off by clutter.
{"headers":["Whiteboard item","MCP equivalent"],"rows":[["A note written on the board","A message, tool result, or resource excerpt"],["Erasing an old note","Trimming stale context"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Context Is Rebuilt Every Turn, Not Persisted by the Model

A model itself has no memory between requests, every single time it is asked to respond, the full relevant context has to be sent to it again, the host is effectively rebuilding a snapshot of everything the model needs to know, fresh, on every single turn.
This might feel wasteful at first glance, but it is exactly what makes each request self-contained and predictable, the model never has to guess what it might or might not still remember.
This rebuilding cost is part of why keeping context lean matters practically too, a larger context sent on every single turn also means more processing time and cost per request.
12. Context vs Memory: Not the Same Thing

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Context lasts this turn while memory persists across turns

blocks.text: Context is what a model sees for one specific request, memory, covered in the Memory Management lesson in the Context Management module, is a longer-lived store of important facts that might persist across many separate sessions, context is rebuilt every turn, memory is deliberately kept around.

A system with good memory but poor context management can still fail, remembering the right fact long-term does no good if it never gets pulled back into context for the specific request that needed it.

Some systems bridge the two deliberately, pulling a relevant fact out of long-term memory and inserting it into context specifically for the request that needs it, rather than keeping everything in context permanently.
Getting this distinction clear early avoids a lot of confusion later, especially when debugging why a model seems to know, or not know, something a previous session covered.
13. A Worked Example
Trace how context accumulates across a short exchange, a resource read, a tool call, and a final model response, all built from what came before.

code.content:
context = []
context.append({"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this file and email it to my manager"})
doc = client.read_resource("file:///report.txt")
context.append({"role": "resource", "content": doc["text"]})
summary = model.generate(context)
context.append({"role": "assistant", "content": summary})
client.call_tool("send_email", {"to": "manager@example.com", "body": summary})

blocks.text: Notice how the resource content and the tool call result both became part of the same growing context, each contributing exactly the information needed for the model to complete its task correctly.

If a second, unrelated user question arrived right after this exchange, a thoughtful host might choose to drop the earlier resource content from context, since it is no longer relevant to what is being asked now.
14. Common Mistakes When Thinking About Context

items: Assuming context is unlimited, and being surprised when a long session suddenly hits a hard size limit.
Reading a very large resource without considering how much of the available context budget it will consume.
Letting stale tool or resource content linger in context long after it stopped being relevant or accurate.
Forgetting that the host, not the model or the server, is responsible for deciding what actually gets included in context.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is confusing context with memory, assuming that because a model mentioned something once, it will automatically remember it in a completely separate future session.

A sixth common mistake is assuming a longer context window means context management no longer matters, even a very large window is still finite, and irrelevant clutter still costs real space and can distract the model’s reasoning.
A seventh common mistake is never measuring actual context usage in a real running system, relying purely on intuition about what is probably fine rather than checking directly.
15. Practice: Trace Your Own Context Budget

Pick a short, realistic multi-step task involving one resource read and one tool call, and list out, step by step, everything that would end up in context by the time the model produces its final response.

code.content:
context_pieces = ["system prompt", "user message", "resource content", "tool result", "assistant reply"]
for piece in context_pieces: print(piece)

blocks.text: Once you have listed these pieces, try estimating roughly how much of the total context budget each one might realistically consume, and consider which one you would trim first if space ran short.

blocks.title: One more thing to try
blocks.content: Repeat the same exercise for a task involving two separate resource reads instead of one, and notice how quickly the context budget question becomes more pressing.

blocks.text: This kind of budgeting exercise, done by hand once or twice, builds real intuition that pays off later when reading actual token usage numbers from a running system.
Key Takeaway

Context is the sum total of everything a model can see when responding, conversation history, tool results, resource content, and prompt framing, all competing for a finite amount of space, deliberately assembled and maintained by the host application rather than something that simply happens on its own.
This lesson closes the tour of what tools, resources, and prompts contribute to a session. The next lesson, Messages, looks at the basic unit all of this communication is actually built from.

The context-versus-memory distinction from the newly added section becomes especially important once you reach the Memory Management lesson later in this curriculum, keep the two concepts clearly separated in your mental model going forward.
